column1: What is a system Python, in uv's terms?
column2: An interpreter already on the machine when uv arrived. uv will use it but never modify it.
One uv downloaded itself into uv's own directory, where uv is free to add and remove.

column1: Does uv download Python versions automatically?
column2: Yes. uv downloads Python versions when they are required.

column1: Which command installs a specific Python?
Which command lists every interpreter uv can see or fetch?
What do the two right-hand column values in uv python list mean?
column2: A real path means the interpreter is already installed; <download available> means uv can fetch it.

column1: Where do uv's Python builds come from?
column2: python-build-standalone — portable builds designed to run from any folder, not python.org.

column1: Why does portability matter for uv's interpreters?
column2: uv can drop the interpreter into its own directory and have it work, without a fixed install location.

column1: Which command pins a project to a Python version?

column2: .python-version, one line of text, meant to be committed.
In the current folder and then every parent folder above it. The nearest one wins.

column1: Your project says requires-python >=3.10 and you have 3.10 and 3.13. Which does uv use?
column2: 3.10 — uv takes the first compatible version, not the newest.

column1: Does uv python install put a bare python command on your PATH?
column2: No, deliberately. Pass --default if you explicitly want that.
.python-version chooses the interpreter you develop on. requires-python is a public promise about what your code supports.

column1: How do you run one command on a different interpreter?
column2: uv run --python 3.9 <command>, which changes nothing you have pinned.

column1: Which command removes a managed Python?
column2: uv python uninstall <version>. System interpreters are never touched.
